findings.paper_title: Full Council - 202526 Revenue Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: £1m provision for Devon Local Government Reorganisation (April 2028) drawn from reserves intended for other needs
findings.detail: The council is establishing a Local Government Reorganisation Reserve of £1.0m to fund Teignbridge's contribution to the Devon LGR programme, funded from the undrawn funding reserve allocation. This is a material one-off cost commitment.
findings.matters: A £1m future cost commitment reduces financial flexibility and, combined with the ongoing structural budget gap, constrains the council's ability to respond to emerging challenges over the next two years.
findings.figures: £1.0m LGR Reserve; LGR implementation date April 2028
findings.quote: It is proposed that £1.000m be transferred into the reserve from the undrawn funding reserve allocation originally included in the budget. The level of funding has been informed by the costs incurred through previous local government reorganisation programmes and reflects the anticipated scale of investment required to support the transition to the new arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Full Council - 202526 Revenue Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: Structural budget gap of £1.1m forecast for 2026/27, to be funded from reserves and further savings identification
findings.detail: Despite achieving a revenue surplus in 2025/26, the council forecasts a £1.1m budget gap in 2026/27 to be met through draw from the Funding Reserve. The paper explicitly states that savings delivered in 2025/26 will not be sufficient and further efficiencies must be identified.
findings.matters: Ongoing reliance on reserve drawdowns to balance budgets and the need to identify further efficiencies indicates a structural imbalance that may persist across the medium-term financial plan, affecting the council's financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £1.1m budget gap; Funding Reserve draw planned for 2026/27
findings.quote: these benefits are not expected to fully close the gap, and the Council will need to continue to identify and deliver further efficiencies, savings and income opportunities to achieve a sustainable balanced budget over the life of the Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP).

findings.paper_title: Full Council - 202526 Revenue Capital and Treasury Outturn
findings.headline: Significant capital project slippage: £6.1m delayed across four major schemes
findings.detail: Actual capital spend in 2025/26 was £14.6m against a reprofiled budget of £22.5m. The four largest delays are: Sherborne House Carpark Housing (£2.4m), Waste Transfer Station Improvements (£2.3m), Market Hall Transformation (£0.7m), and Dawlish Leisure Centre Refurbishment (£0.7m). The council attributes this to project delays rather than underspends.
findings.matters: Capital delivery slippage across named major schemes signals execution risk and suggests the council may struggle to deliver its expanded 2026/27 capital programme (£33.4m), which a lender would need to assess as funded and deliverable.
findings.figures: £14.6m actual vs £22.5m reprofiled budget; individual delays: £2.4m, £2.3m, £0.7m, £0.7m
findings.quote: Actual spend totalled £14.6m which was primarily due to delays with projects rather than project underspends.

findings.headline: Data governance maturity is below expected standards with recommendations from LGA assessment still being implemented
findings.detail: The Council's data management capabilities were assessed under the LGA Data 360 maturity pilot, identifying gaps that require strengthening. Data governance is flagged as an area needing improvement, particularly important ahead of LGR when IT systems must integrate with counterparts.
findings.matters: Weak data governance affects the reliability of financial information, quality of internal controls, and the Council's ability to execute the technical integration required for Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Improving data governance in preparation for LGR and in line with the recommendations from the LGA Data Maturity pilot assessment.

findings.headline: Member conduct problems were systematic enough to warrant independent expert investigation into underlying causes
findings.detail: The Council commissioned a qualified expert to investigate underlying causes of member behaviours (not isolated incidents), with the review reported to Full Council in May 2026. This was part of wider governance improvements including committee restructuring and audit term updates.
findings.matters: Systematic member conduct issues that required external investigation suggest governance control weaknesses, though reduction in complaints from 61 to 34 indicates improvement.
findings.figures: Code of conduct complaints: 34 in 2025-26 (down from 61 in prior year)
findings.quote: A Member Conduct Review was commissioned, conducted by a suitably qualified expert to investigate the underlying causes of member behaviours. This reported to Full Council in May 2026 and was agreed.

findings.headline: Budget gap remains unresolved despite three-year funding settlement and delivered savings
findings.detail: Despite improved certainty from a three-year government funding settlement and service savings already delivered, the Council states further savings are required to close the budget gap. This suggests structural imbalance between revenue and expenditure.
findings.matters: Persistent structural deficit even after savings efforts and improved funding certainty indicates underlying financial pressure that may constrain the Council's ability to service debt.
findings.figures: Specific gap size not disclosed
findings.quote: Service savings have been delivered which has reduced the budget gap, but further savings are required in order to close it.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will transform Teignbridge into a Devon unitary authority in May 2028, requiring parallel operations and transition management for two years
findings.detail: The Council is facing merger into a new unitary authority, a major structural change requiring work programmes, revised decision-making processes, and management attention to both current operations and transition activities. This directly impacts the resources available for normal Council business.
findings.matters: A lender would need to assess the operational risk and management capacity constraints during a two-year transition period, and the Council's ability to maintain financial stability and service delivery through that period.
findings.figures: Transition date: May 2028
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation will impact on the Council's resources and priorities. The Council will need to continue operating as an organisation whilst preparing to become a Unitary Authority alongside other Councils in Devon in May 2028.

findings.paper_title: Q4 Audit Scrutiny 27.06.26 - Strategic & Corporate Risk Report
findings.headline: A critical staffing role (Elections Coordinator) is currently vacant with no dedicated resource identified for replacement.
findings.detail: Election management (ST20) is listed as a high unmitigated risk (15) with a high mitigated score (8) even after safeguards. The notes record: 'Elections coordinator post currently vacant due to retirement, resource to be appointed.' The risk of a poorly managed election includes 'embarrassment, loss of reputation and High Court challenge.' A vacant role during peak election season is a control gap.
findings.matters: Electoral failure is reputational and legal. A vacant coordinator means election planning is running under-resourced, increasing the likelihood of the named risks materializing.
findings.figures: Mitigated risk score 8 (Medium) for ST20
findings.quote: Elections coordinator post currently vacant due to retirement, resource to be appointed.

findings.paper_title: Q4 Audit Scrutiny 27.06.26 - Strategic & Corporate Risk Report
findings.headline: Economic uncertainty is rated as a structural financial risk with no further mitigation planned beyond budget monitoring and reserves.
findings.detail: Economic Uncertainty (ST08) carries both an unmitigated and mitigated score of 9 (Medium). The risk scenario is clear: 'Changes to the macro-economic situation will impact upon our ability to deliver our Council Strategy and may lead to increased unemployment, a collapse of the housing market and an increased demand on Council services e.g. housing benefits.' The mitigations listed are standard: budget monitoring, reserves held, and financial management. There is no action indicating preparation for a sustained downturn.
findings.matters: A council acknowledging it cannot mitigate economic downturn beyond holding reserves is a council exposed to income volatility. Combined with the Finance Control risk, this suggests limited headroom for budget pressure.
findings.figures: Reserves held: ~£2.4m
findings.quote: Changes to the macro-economic situation will impact upon our ability to deliver our Council Strategy and may lead to increased unemployment, a collapse of the housing market and an increased demand on Council services e.g. housing benefits.

findings.paper_title: Q4 Audit Scrutiny 27.06.26 - Strategic & Corporate Risk Report
findings.headline: The council's risk management system cannot generate automated review reminders due to software compatibility issues, degrading governance.
findings.detail: The corporate Risk Management Strategy (CP16) is flagged as needing review. In the notes for CP16, it is stated that 'The functionality of the SPAR.net risk management system is not compatible with the version of Microsoft now in use; whilst a workaround has been established it is not currently possible to generate automated risk review reminders, and a system upgrade may be needed.' This means risk reviews (which are supposed to happen monthly for very high risks, quarterly for high, biannually for medium) are now manual processes subject to human failure.
findings.matters: Risk management is mandated by law. A council unable to automate risk review reminders is at risk of missed or overdue reviews, particularly of very high risks like H&S and cyber security.
findings.figures: Risk management score: Mitigated 8 (Medium); two 'Action needed' items flagged
findings.quote: The functionality of the SPAR.net risk management system is not compatible with the version of Microsoft now in use; whilst a workaround has been established it is not currently possible to generate automated risk review reminders, and a system upgrade may be needed.

findings.paper_title: Q4 Audit Scrutiny 27.06.26 - Strategic & Corporate Risk Report
findings.headline: Finance control and budget management carry structural risk that remains unresolved despite mitigations.
findings.detail: Finance control (ST02) is explicitly listed as a strategic financial risk. The unmitigated score is 15 (High); the mitigated score is 8 (Medium). The risk is described as 'Budget restraints/lack of finances, due to local & national changes in service demand that effect levels of spend or income leading to a budget imbalance.' The document notes that controls include reserves (~£2.4m) and budget monitoring, but the risk itself remains present and requires ongoing mitigation.
findings.matters: This is the council declaring that budget imbalance is a live risk. Combined with economic uncertainty (also listed as a structural financial risk), this flags the council's financial resilience as uncertain.
findings.figures: Reserves: ~£2.4m maintained
findings.quote: Budget restraints/lack of finances, due to local & national changes in service demand that effect levels of spend or income leading to a budget imbalance

findings.paper_title: Q4 Audit Scrutiny 27.06.26 - Strategic & Corporate Risk Report
findings.headline: Multiple Health and Safety compliance actions are flagged as needed rather than ongoing, leaving a gap between policy and evidence.
findings.detail: Health & Safety (ST11) carries an unmitigated risk score of 20 (very high), and even after mitigations sits at 12 (high). The risk review notes that managers cannot evidence identification of training needs or effective refresher provision, and the competency framework requirement remains unmitigated. The Audit Committee notes specifically: 'unable to evidence identification and or effective provision and refreshers - competency framework requirement is not mitigated.' Multiple mitigations are marked 'Action needed' (not 'Action ongoing'): Adequate H&S resources, Approved Policies and procedures, H&S training, Risk assessments, and Safety audits.
findings.matters: H&S non-compliance creates potential corporate manslaughter liability, prosecution risk, and high insurance costs. A council unable to evidence its own compliance controls is a control weakness a lender needs to understand.
findings.figures: Unmitigated risk score 20 (Very High); Mitigated risk score 12 (High)
findings.quote: unable to evidence identification and or effective provision and refreshers - competency framework requirement is not mitigated

findings.headline: CIL income posting errors identified between Exacom and FMS systems; correction process incomplete
findings.detail: From prior year Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) income testing in grants and debtors, auditors identified a number of errors in postings between the Exacom system and FMS system. This issue was flagged as in-progress with no indication of completion.
findings.matters: CIL is material income to councils; posting errors between systems indicate weak reconciliation controls and data integrity risks that could mask revenue misstatement.
findings.figures: Multiple errors identified in CIL postings
findings.quote: From our CIL income testing in grants and debtors, we have identified a number of errors in the postings between the Exacom system and FMS system.

findings.headline: Related party declarations not updated annually; some last reviewed two years prior
findings.detail: In the prior audit review of related parties, the council was found to have instances where declarations in the Register of Interests were last updated two years ago and do not reflect an annual confirmation process. While the council sends annual reminders with links to the declarations form, the process is not ensuring annual refreshes.
findings.matters: Related party disclosures are fundamental to financial statement integrity and audit reliance. Non-annual certification indicates weak governance over conflict of interest management and related party identification.
findings.figures: Declarations last updated 2 years prior in some instances
findings.quote: we have identified a number of instances where the declarations in the Register of Interests were last updated two years ago and do not reflect an annual confirmation process.

findings.headline: Asset depreciation and valuation control failures: 6 assets with negative carrying values; 87 with improper residual balances
findings.detail: Audit identified 6 assets with negative carrying values because they continued to depreciate after becoming fully depreciated, and 87 assets left with small residual balances instead of being fully depreciated or cleared. Although residual amounts were below the trivial threshold, assets should be properly managed to zero or disposal.
findings.matters: Depreciation errors indicate weak fixed asset controls and compromise the reliability of the balance sheet. This compounds the prior-year disclaimer on land and buildings valuation.
findings.figures: 6 assets with negative carrying values; 87 assets with improper residual balances
findings.quote: we identified six assets with negative carrying values due to an extra year of depreciation being charged after the asset was fully depreciated. We also identified 87 assets being left with small residual balances instead of being fully depreciated or cleared on disposal.

findings.headline: Finance system age and capacity constraints: only one staff member can extract required reports
findings.detail: The audit identifies that the council's finance system is old and user-unfriendly, with only one Finance Systems Analyst/Administrator able to integrate the system and pull financial reports. During the prior audit, this individual was seconded to a project, preventing the finance team from providing required audit reports such as trial balance and general ledger. A data migration from Strata servers to Microsoft servers is planned for December 2025.
findings.matters: A single point of failure in finance reporting capability creates operational risk and audit delay. Reliance on one person also creates fraud risk and business continuity vulnerability. Migration to new infrastructure during an audit year adds further risk.
findings.figures: One Finance Systems Analyst/Administrator; data migration scheduled December 2025
findings.quote: The audit was delayed by the age and user-friendliness of the finance system as there is typically only one member of the finance team the Finance Systems Analyst/Administrator, who can integrate the system and pull-down financial reports.

findings.headline: Capital programme £6.8m with material capital additions; risk of fraudulent capitalisation of revenue items
findings.detail: The council's capital programme totals £6.8m with material capital additions. Auditors specifically flag a fraud risk that the council could manipulate year-end impact on the general fund through inappropriate capitalisation of revenue items as capital expenditure, though they do not assess this as a significant risk due to low fraud risk in the nature of underlying transactions.
findings.matters: Capital accounting manipulation is a mechanism councils can use to artificially improve revenue position. The auditor's flag of this specific risk (despite not rating it significant) suggests the council's asset capitalisation controls warrant scrutiny.
findings.figures: Capital programme £6.8m; material level of capital additions
findings.quote: During the year ended 31 March 2025 the Council's capital programme was £6.8m, with a material level of capital additions. Therefore, if the Council were to fraudulently recognise expenditure, we believe it would be through the inappropriate capitalisation of revenue items.

findings.headline: Three significant weaknesses identified in value for money arrangements relating to governance and decision-making
findings.detail: Auditors identified three risks of significant weakness in VFM arrangements: standards of behaviour, incorrect governance processes, and arrangements for decision making and high profile capital projects. These relate to findings from 2023/24 (member behaviour, member involvement in council business, decision-making processes) that were followed up in 2024/25. A statutory recommendation from 2023/24 is retained and progress is being monitored.
findings.matters: Persistent governance weaknesses across member behaviour, process integrity, and capital decision-making represent institutional control failures. Lenders assess council governance as a credit risk factor; unresolved governance issues indicate weak institutional controls.
findings.figures: 3 identified risks; statutory recommendation retained from 2023/24
findings.quote: Three risks of significant weakness identified. These risks relate to findings from 2023/24 work that were followed up in 2024/25, specifically in relation to member behaviour, involvement of members in council business, and decision-making processes.

findings.headline: Eleven prior year audit recommendations remain unimplemented, including payroll, systems, and asset controls
findings.detail: The audit identifies 11 recommendations from 2024/25 still to be addressed and carried forward from 2023/24, covering a former employee remaining on payroll for four months post-departure, trial balance non-reconciliation, asset valuations outside the 5-year rolling programme (101 assets worth £1.3m not revalued since 2019), and lack of a formal de minimis limit for expenditure. Finance system constraints prevent required data extraction format.
findings.matters: Unresolved prior-year audit findings indicate weak implementation of control improvements. These include payroll integrity risks, asset valuation compliance breaches, and system limitations that compound year on year.
findings.figures: 11 recommendations in progress; 101 assets (£1.3m) valued outside 5-year period; potential asset movement £185k; informal de minimis of £1k
findings.quote: 11 are still to be addressed

findings.headline: Disclaimer of opinion in prior year means no assurance over closing reserves balance for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council received a disclaimer of opinion in 2024/25 due to the backstop deadline, with a specific disclaimer linked to Property, Plant and Equipment revaluation (also disclaimed in 2020/21). As a result, auditors will have limited assurance over opening balances for 2025/26 and no assurance over closing reserves balance due to uncertainty over their opening amount. Auditors are working towards recovering assurance over in-year transactions but will need full council cooperation.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion on reserves is a fundamental audit weakness that prevents any reliable financial reporting position. Lenders depend on audited accounts; absence of assurance over reserve balances is material to credit assessment.
findings.figures: Opening balances uncertain; closing reserves balance unassured due to prior year disclaimer
findings.quote: we will have limited assurance over the opening balances for 2025/26; and no assurance over the closing reserves balance, due to the uncertainty over their opening amount.

findings.headline: Capital programme is planned to be funded through prudential borrowing, though revenue borrowing is not expected in the next two years
findings.detail: The council intends to finance capital projects over the next three years using capital receipts, grants, prudential borrowing, and developer contributions. Major projects (Teignbridge 100, Dawlish Leisure Centre, Carbon Action Plan employment sites) are explicitly to be funded through prudential borrowing. The CFO states 'it is anticipated, dependent upon progress of the town centre developments and the Teignbridge 100, that external borrowing will not be required in the next two years.' This is conditional on project performance.
findings.matters: Prudential borrowing adds interest cost and MRP (Minimum Revenue Provision) to the revenue budget, increasing structural costs. The conditional language suggests uncertainty about whether borrowing will actually be avoided. Business cases 'rely on forecasts for rental income', creating revenue risk if projects underperform.
findings.figures: Prudential borrowing planned for capital projects; interest rate risk flagged; no external borrowing expected for next two years (if projects progress)
findings.quote: It is anticipated, dependent upon progress of the town centre developments and the Teignbridge 100, that external borrowing will not be required in the next two years. Slippage in the capital programme can mean usable reserves stay higher for longer, delaying the need to borrow.

findings.headline: Business rates safety-net protection is reducing year-on-year, exposing the council to greater downside risk
findings.detail: The Business Rates Retention Scheme includes a safety net that protects councils from income falls. For 2026/27, this is 100% protection. However, it reduces to 97% in 2027/28 and 92.5% in 2028/29, the final year of the new rating list. This means the council's exposure to business rates shortfalls increases progressively over the medium term.
findings.matters: Declining protection means the council will absorb a larger share of any business rates downturn. Combined with already-low reserves, this is an increasing risk headwind.
findings.quote: For 2026/27, a 100% safety net will apply, under which Government will fully compensate any shortfall in funding below the baseline level. This protection reduces to 97% in 2027/28 and 92.5% in 2028/29, the final year of the new rating list.

findings.headline: New Homes Bonus funding stream has been scrapped, removing a recurring source of income
findings.detail: The council has historically received New Homes Bonus income 'on the extra homes built per year and a 4 year payment'. The multi-year settlement has confirmed this has been scrapped for 2026/27 and future years. This is a permanent loss of income that must be absorbed or compensated through the budget.
findings.matters: Loss of a recurring grant funding stream reduces overall income available to the council. The impact must come from service reductions, reserves, or other compensating income growth.
findings.figures: New Homes Bonus scrapped from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: New homes bonus has traditionally been estimated on the extra homes built per year and a 4 year payment. The multi year settlement has confirmed that New Homes Bonus has been scrapped for 2026/27 and future years.

findings.headline: Council tax collection risk increasing as provision for non-collection rises and council tax increases by 5.2%
findings.detail: The council has increased its provision for council tax collection losses from 2.1% to 2.2% in 2026/27, explicitly citing concern about 'continuing economic circumstances which is likely to be more difficult next year'. This is coupled with the council imposing a 5.2% overall council tax increase, which could further strain collection rates among households already struggling with bills.
findings.matters: Rising collection risk and rising council tax charges together signal the council expects household payment difficulties to increase. This is a leading indicator of income stress and creates pressure on the reserve.
findings.figures: Council tax collection loss provision increased from 2.1% to 2.2%; council tax increase 5.2% for 2026/27
findings.quote: The small provision of 2.1% which has traditionally been made for potential losses in council tax collection has been increased in 2026/27 to 2.2% to reflect continuing economic circumstances which is likely to be more difficult next year with the estimated overall increase of 5.2% in council tax.

findings.headline: Income budget of £18.4m includes significant Market Walk rental income with a material downside risk of £1.8m
findings.detail: The council assumes £18.4m in 2026/27 from sales, fees, charges, recycling, and property income. The document explicitly flags that this 'includes significant rental income from Market Walk' and notes there is 'always the risk that income could fall further or be less than anticipated'. A 10% drop in income against the net budget would result in a loss of £1,838,000—more than half the general revenue reserve.
findings.matters: Income from a single property asset (Market Walk) is concentrated risk. A vacancy, tenant default, or valuation correction could create a £1.8m shortfall that would be difficult to absorb given low reserve levels.
findings.figures: £18.4m total income budget 2026/27; 10% income drop = £1,838,000 shortfall
findings.quote: The budget assumes £18.4 million of income from sales, fees and charges, recycling and property for 2026/27. Whilst this assumption is realistic for the income it includes significant rental income from Market Walk and there is always the risk that income could fall further or be less than anticipated. A drop in income as compared to the net budget of around 10% would result in a loss of £1,838,000.

findings.headline: Savings plan of £2.6m annually is essential to the budget but is flagged as a key risk if not delivered
findings.detail: The 'Modern 25' agenda targets £2.6m in annual ongoing savings through organisational restructuring, asset review, and service activity savings. The CFO's conclusion explicitly identifies 'non delivery of required savings' as one of the 'main financial risks'. The savings are being 'mapped out, reported and updated regularly' by the Business Transformation Team, suggesting they are not yet locked in.
findings.matters: If the £2.6m savings plan slips or fails to deliver, the council will need to find additional funding from reserves or cut services further. Combined with the reserve depletion already planned, failure to deliver savings would accelerate the timing of reserve exhaustion.
findings.figures: £2.6m annual savings target from Modern 25 agenda
findings.quote: The Modern 25 agenda looks at a savings plan which delivers ongoing annual savings totalling £2.6 million which included the revision of our organisational structure to deliver staff savings, a review of our assets and how they are used and other service activity savings options. The savings 'drops' are mapped out, reported and updated regularly and managed by the Business Transformation Team.

findings.headline: Reserve levels are low relative to peer councils, placing Teignbridge at higher financial stress risk
findings.detail: CIPFA's Resilience Index benchmarking shows Teignbridge has a reserves-to-revenue expenditure ratio of 100.87%, placing it towards the lower end of its peer group. The nearest neighbours range from 40.57% (lowest) to 443.09% (highest). This low reserve position is explicitly flagged as the 'highest-risk indicator' in the CIPFA assessment and contributes to 'higher-risk assessment for this indicator'.
findings.matters: Low reserves reduce a council's ability to absorb unexpected cost pressures or income shocks. Lenders assess reserve adequacy as a core measure of financial resilience.
findings.figures: Teignbridge reserves-to-revenue ratio 100.87%; peer range 40.57%–443.09%
findings.quote: The highest‑risk indicator is the level of reserves. Teignbridge had a reserves-to-revenue expenditure ratio of 100.87%, compared with a range among our nearest neighbours of: 443.09% (highest‑reserves neighbour), 40.57% (lowest‑reserves neighbour). This places Teignbridge towards the lower end of reserve levels within the group, contributing to the higher‑risk assessment for this indicator.

findings.headline: Structural budget deficits being covered by drawing down an earmarked reserve scheduled to deplete over four years
findings.detail: The council faces revenue budget overspends documented in appendix 4. Rather than balance the budget through service cuts or revenue raising, it is using a Funding Earmarked Reserve that held £11.7m at the start of 2025/26. The plan is to draw £4.8m from this reserve over the four years 2025/26 to 2028/29. The CFO notes that 'even with no further action' the reserve 'can be utilised to manage the deficits anticipated up to the end of the MTFP', but this approach is finite.
findings.matters: A council running deficits and funding them from a reserve that is being depleted is not sustainable. This signals structural budget imbalance, not a temporary problem.
findings.figures: Funding Earmarked Reserve £11.7m at start 2025/26; £4.8m to be used 2025/26–2028/29
findings.quote: The savings required to eliminate our revenue budget overspends within our MTFP are detailed in appendix 4. These are currently funded by a Funding Earmarked Reserve that had a balance of £11.7 million at the start of the 2025/26 financial year and even with no further action can be utilised to manage the deficits anticipated up to the end of the MTFP.

findings.headline: Provisional schemes risk materially accelerating borrowing timeline and costs if approved
findings.detail: The capital programme includes provisional schemes not yet approved. If these are approved, the borrowing requirement and associated costs would 'significantly increase and bring forward' the date when external borrowing is needed. This represents a major contingent liability.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that the council's borrowing profile has material upside risk depending on capital investment decisions yet to be made.
findings.figures: Provisional schemes currently add £0.357m to 2025-26 capital requirement but cumulative impact not separately quantified
findings.quote: It should be noted that should provisional schemes be approved, this will significantly increase and bring forward the need to borrow and associated costs.

findings.headline: Currently foregoing £1.1m annual investment income by using internal borrowing rather than external debt
findings.detail: The council is choosing to use cash reserves to fund capital rather than borrow externally. This costs the council approximately £1.1m per year in foregone investment income. Once external borrowing begins, this saving disappears and the council will incur actual interest expense instead.
findings.matters: The calculation shows the trade-off the council has made and confirms that external borrowing will create a material new revenue charge once reserves are depleted.
findings.figures: Interest foregone £1,102,575 per annum (average for April to November 2024-25); would have cost £1,135,336 per annum if externally borrowed at PWLB rates as of 1 April 2024
findings.quote: Based on the average treasury management interest rate received during April to November 2024-25, interest foregone due to internal borrowing to cover the Council's Capital Financing Requirement would be in the region of £1,102,575 per annum.

findings.headline: Council depleting internal reserves rapidly to fund capital, forcing accelerated external borrowing
findings.detail: Internal borrowing (use of cash reserves) declines from £40.955m in 2026-27 to £23.449m by 2029-30, a fall of 43%. This accelerated depletion of reserves is what makes external borrowing inevitable. The capital programme is structured on the assumption that reserves can absorb this level of drawdown.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion leaves no buffer for unexpected pressures or downside scenarios. A lender needs to understand the council's reserve position will be substantially weaker by 2029-30.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £40.955m (2026-27) falling to £23.449m (2029-30); equivalent reduction to £5.8m minimum liquidity buffer by 2028-29
findings.quote: Estimated internal borrowing based on forecast usable reserves/leases funded from revenue budgets: -40,955 [-2026-27] reducing to -23,449 [-2029-30]

findings.headline: Commercial property income equals 219% of general reserves; any downturn would create severe financial stress
findings.detail: Net income from the council's commercial and service investments (mainly property) represented 219% of un-earmarked general revenue reserves in 2024-25. This extreme ratio means the council's annual investment income exceeds its total liquid reserves. A significant fall in property values, rental income, or market conditions would create material financial difficulty.
findings.matters: A lender should understand the council's vulnerability to property market conditions and tenant default risk, given this heavy dependency on property income.
findings.figures: 219% of general reserves in 2024-25; gross rental income £8.737m; net income after costs £5.483m
findings.quote: Net income from commercial and service investments in 2024-25 as a percentage of these general reserves was 219%.

findings.headline: Proportional debt limit cut by £10 million to reflect interest rate risks
findings.detail: The commercial debt limit has been reduced from a higher level to £60 million. This reduction is explicitly attributed to 'current interest rate risks'. This tightening of the council's own debt constraint signals concern about future borrowing costs.
findings.matters: A lender should be alert to why the council is reducing its own debt headroom, and what this indicates about expected future interest rates.
findings.figures: Proportional debt limit £60 million; represents 'around three times the Council's core spending power'
findings.quote: The reduction of £10 million compared to earlier years reflects current interest rate risks and maintains maximum borrowing at around three times the Council's core spending power.

findings.headline: External borrowing now expected within three years, ending current debt-free position
findings.detail: The council currently funds capital expenditure from internal reserves with zero external borrowing. The Capital Financing Requirement forecast shows this will end by 2028-29, when external borrowing becomes likely, and possibly from end of 2027-28. This marks a material change in the council's debt profile and financing costs.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand when the council will first enter the external debt market and how this will affect its debt service coverage and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement £39.2m in 2025-26, declining to £36.4m by 2029-30; external borrowing forecast £11.6m by 2028-29
findings.quote: At this stage, external borrowing appears likely by 2028-29 and possible towards the end of 2027-28.

findings.headline: Capital receipts exhausted by 2025/26; £15.8m new borrowing required by 2029/32 on top of £35.4m underlying need
findings.detail: The council notes 'General Fund capital receipts largely being used by 2025/26'. The capital programme assumes £15.8m of new borrowing between 2025/26-2029/32, in addition to an existing underlying borrowing need of £35.4m. Though 'no immediate need to borrow externally over the next 2-3 years' due to cash flow, future borrowing costs will compound the revenue position and depend on interest rate environment.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council's capital ambitions are sustainable given the revenue budget stress. Rising borrowing costs (already mentioned as a risk) directly feed into revenue pressures. Capital receipts depletion removes one asset-based solution.
findings.figures: £15.8m new borrowing 2025/26–2029/32; £35.4m underlying borrowing need; capital receipts exhausted 2025/26; revenue contributions to capital drop from £1.5m (2025/26–2026/27) to £500k (future years)
findings.quote: The programme assumes £15.8 million of borrowing between 2025/26 and 2029/32 in addition to the current underlying need to borrow of £35.4 million. Cash flow monitoring and balance sheet review exercises indicate no immediate need to borrow externally over the next 2 - 3 years.

findings.headline: Pay structure review underway to 'remain competitive' — signals wage cost pressure
findings.detail: The council is undertaking a pay and job evaluation review to 'ensure the Council remains competitive and can attract the staff with the key skills'. The 2026/27 budget assumes a 3% pay increase with 'final offer to be determined at a later date'. This suggests potential for slippage above 3% if market conditions tighten, directly feeding into budget shortfalls.
findings.matters: Staff costs typically represent 50%+ of district council budgets. A pay review that aims to become 'competitive' suggests the council is concerned about recruitment and retention. Actual settlement above 3% would worsen the shortfall position materially.
findings.figures: 3% assumed increase for 2026/27; final offer not yet determined
findings.quote: The Council has also undertaking a pay structure review which will result in a new pay scale and job evaluation process being developed and implemented to ensure the Council remains competitive and can attract the staff with the key skills to deliver the best service for residents in the District.

findings.headline: Modern 25 transformation programme must deliver £2.6m savings or financial position deteriorates
findings.detail: A major organisational restructure is underway with new operating model, digital transformation, and staff reorganisation. The council is targeting £2.6m of 'phased benefit savings'. New structure has been approved and implemented with posts 'advertised and appointed'. If this programme underperforms, the shortfall gap widens and reserve depletion accelerates.
findings.matters: This is the council's primary lever to close the budget gap. If Modern 25 delivers less than £2.6m, or delivers it more slowly than projected, the council has limited other options. Transformation risk is significant given the council's dependence on success.
findings.figures: £2.6m targeted phased benefit savings
findings.quote: From their recommendation we have developed our Modern 25 programme which aims to deliver a new operating model for the council delivering £2.6 million of phased benefit savings and implementing the changes across the whole council in line with agreed design principles. The organisation restructure has been approved and has now been implemented and posts advertised and appointed.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves being drawn down to bridge budget gaps with no buffer for shocks
findings.detail: The council explicitly relies on 'use of earmarked funding reserves' to balance budgets 'but by exception'. If savings are not found over the next three years, 'the Funding Reserve will continue to be depleted leaving insufficient funds to address future significant variations in funding or budget pressures elsewhere including the capital programme.' This creates a hard deadline for savings delivery.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council is running down reserves sustainably or approaching insolvency. Depletion to zero means the council has no buffer for a funding shock, staff cost spike, or capital emergency.
findings.figures: £1.126m–£1.623m annual shortfalls projected to run against reserves for 3+ years
findings.quote: If savings are not found over the next 3 years, then the Funding Reserve will continue to be depleted leaving insufficient funds to address future significant variations in funding or budget pressures elsewhere including the capital programme.

findings.headline: New Homes Bonus discontinued and business rates baseline reset strips away £3.5m+ in accumulated funding
findings.detail: The council received £3.848m from NHB in 2016/17 but only £0.35m by 2025/26; it is now discontinued. Simultaneously, the 2026/27 business rates baseline reset removes accumulated growth from prior years. The document states 'pooling arrangements with the other Devon Authorities are no longer beneficial' — a structural funding loss the council cannot control.
findings.matters: This represents permanent loss of revenue-raising capacity that historically put Teignbridge in a stronger position than peer councils. The reset happens in the same year the budget gaps materialize, compounding the financial stress.
findings.figures: New Homes Bonus 2016/17: £3.848m → 2025/26: £0.35m → 2026/27: £0 (discontinued). Business rates baseline reset 2026/27.
findings.quote: New Homes Bonus has been discontinued for 2026/27 and the nationally, this funding has been re-distributed within the Revenue Support Grant, using new funding formulas. At the height of the scheme the Council was paid the annual growth sum for 6 years – in 2016/17 the Council received £3.848 million (the most received in any one year). For 2025/26 the council received £0.35 million.

findings.headline: Cumulative budget shortfalls of £6.3m over six years with no balance point in sight
findings.detail: The MTFP projects annual shortfalls every year from 2025/26 to 2030/31, ranging from £951k to £1,623k. The largest gap is £1,623k in 2029/30. The council notes these 'shortfalls between the Council's spending requirements and the amount of finance available' require action to address, with further savings needed 'in time for the new unitary's anticipated vesting' — indicating dependency on structural change.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this council can close the gap through savings and service efficiencies, or whether larger structural solutions (merger, service reduction) are the only option. Six-year cumulative gap of this size signals material financial stress.
findings.quote: The Model identifies the pressures and influences on the Council's revenue budgets and highlights a shortfall between the Council's spending requirements and the amount of finance available.

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Accounts production significantly delayed; published 4 July against 30 June statutory deadline
findings.detail: Accounts were published four days late (4 July 2025 vs 30 June deadline) due to resource availability issues, implementation of a new accounting standard, delays in receipt of asset valuations from external providers, and complexity of producing group accounts incorporating Strata transactions.
findings.matters: Missed statutory deadlines and the underlying resource constraints driving them indicate potential broader capacity issues in financial management.
findings.figures: 4 days late; deadline missed by 4 July publication
findings.quote: We published on 4 July 2025 – slightly later than the prescribed date due to significant challenges to produce the accounts including availab ility of resources, implementation of a new accounting standard, delays in receipt of asset valuations from external providers

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Virgin Media contingent liability creating changes to pension valuations
findings.detail: Changes to pension liability valuations have been made to account for a Virgin Media case and its potential impact on the council's pension obligations. The specific financial magnitude of this exposure is not disclosed in this paper.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are typically the largest balance sheet obligation for councils; changes to valuations affect the reported financial position and future cash requirements.
findings.figures: Pension liability valuations adjusted for Virgin Media case (amount unspecified)
findings.quote: there are some changes to the notes to the accounts in relation to pensions and contingent liabilities in relation to a case related to Virgin Media and its potential impact on the values contained within the pension liability

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Full audit not completed: resource availability and competing priorities limited scope significantly
findings.detail: A full audit was not possible due to resource constraints and the audit clashing with budget preparation work. Backstop deadline requirements further reduced materiality thresholds, meaning auditors had to test substantially larger sample sizes in all areas, compounding the resource strain. The accounts must be signed off by 27 February 2026 under backstop arrangements.
findings.matters: Resource constraints preventing full audit suggest capacity issues at the council and create gaps in the verification of controls and transactions that lenders and finance directors rely on.
findings.figures: Partial audit; sample sizes increased significantly; approval deadline 27 February 2026
findings.quote: There has been a partial audit of the 2024/25 statement of accounts...this was due to a number of factors including availability of resources, the audit clashing with the work required to prepare the annual budget proposals. Added to that the complications of back stop dates to accounts preparation reduced the materiality thresholds for the auditors meaning the sample sizes in all areas remain increased significantly

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Auditors issued a disclaimed opinion due to opening balance uncertainties and partial audit completion
findings.detail: The external auditors (Grant Thornton) have issued a disclaimed opinion, meaning they cannot express a view on the accuracy of the reported financial position. This is due to opening balance uncertainties that could not be verified and incomplete audit work. A disclaimed opinion is a significant limitation on the credibility of the accounts.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means the council's opening financial position could not be independently verified, creating uncertainty about the starting point for 2024/25 and affecting confidence in reported balances.
findings.figures: Opening balance verification not completed; full audit opinion disclaimed
findings.quote: We understand the audit opinion will be a 'disclaimed' opinion due to opening balance uncertainties and a partial completion of the audit.

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Governance failure: councillor disqualification not declared vacant promptly as required by law; minor employee fraud case
findings.detail: During the audit, management informed auditors of a governance matter where a councillor who became disqualified was not declared vacant by the council promptly as required by legislation. The seat has since been declared vacant. Additionally, the council reported a minor employee fraud case that has been addressed; auditors consider the amount trivial.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with statutory requirements for councillor vacancy declaration indicates weakness in governance and legal awareness; employee fraud, even if trivial now, raises internal control concerns.
findings.figures: One disqualified councillor not declared vacant promptly; one minor employee fraud case
findings.quote: During the audit, we were informed of a governance matter where a councillor was disqualified, and the seat was not declared vacant promptly as required by legislation. The seat has since been declared vacant... During the course of our audit procedures, we were informed by management of a minor case of employee fraud. The matter has been addressed by the council, and the amount involved is considered trivial.

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Financial system limitations restricting audit interrogation; dependency on single staff member for system administration continues unresolved
findings.detail: The auditors encountered ongoing challenges with the council's finance system, including limited digital working papers and reporting restrictions that prevented audit teams accessing needed data. This dependency on scanned documents and a single Finance Systems Analyst/Administrator for system integration persists from prior year. The individual is frequently seconded to other projects, limiting availability.
findings.matters: System limitations and single-person dependencies create operational risk and delay external audit completion; inability to readily extract finance data indicates weak system controls and creates bottleneck risk if the key person leaves.
findings.figures: System challenges ongoing from 2023/24; audit delayed
findings.quote: We have encountered challenges during the audit due to the continued use of scanned documents and limited digital audit working papers. The financial system in use by the Council has also hindered our interrogation of the finance system as the data we need to be able to complete our work has not been readily available due to the reporting limitations of the current software being used

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Prior period adjustment for SANGS land purchase; initially presented without required third balance sheet
findings.detail: The council is making a prior period adjustment (restating 2021/22 accounts) because land purchased for Suitable Alternative Natural Green Space (SANGS) was incorrectly capitalized. The auditors had flagged this in 2021/22; the council now agrees and is reclassifying as revenue. However, the draft accounts initially omitted the required third balance sheet for 2022/23, which the council has now included after audit challenge.
findings.matters: This is a multi-year accounting error affecting comparative figures; the need for a prior period adjustment indicates weakness in accounting treatment evaluation and the initial omission of disclosure suggests incomplete financial statement preparation.
findings.figures: SANGS transaction entered 2021/22; prior period adjustment now in 2024/25
findings.quote: The council purchased land to use as Suitable Alternative Natural Green Space (SANGS). This transaction was entered into in 21/22 and treated as capital, in our 21/22 Audit Findings Report we reported that we believed SANGS did not meet the definition of capital expenditure. In 24/25 the council have agreed to an alternative method of treatment which aligns with our view as external auditors.

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Fixed asset valuation compliance breached; 101 assets totalling £1.3m outside required 5-year revaluation cycle
findings.detail: The council has 101 assets worth £1.3m that were last valued on 1 April 2019 and not revalued until 31 March 2025, exceeding the CIPFA-mandated 5-year rolling programme. The council attributes this to a change in valuation date from April to March. Although the auditors estimate potential movement of only £185k, this indicates non-compliance with accounting standards.
findings.matters: Breaching mandated valuation cycles creates risk that asset values are materially misstated; the £1.3m balance is material and should not be outside audit procedures for 6 years.
findings.figures: 101 assets; £1.3m total value; £185k estimated potential movement; last valued 1 April 2019
findings.quote: We have identified 101 assets totalling £1.3million that were last valued on 1/04/2019 and not revalued until 31/03/2025. This is therefore outside of the 5-year period, this has occurred due to change in the valuation date in 2024/25 to March from April.

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Unadjusted misstatements totalling £643k cumulatively include pension liability understatement and debtor provision errors
findings.detail: The council has not adjusted for several identified misstatements: an NNDR debtors provision error of £136k, a pension fund assets understatement of £363k (based on the Devon Pension Fund auditor's findings), and a projected creditor over-accrual of £589k from prior year. Cumulative impact across years is £643k affecting the balance sheet.
findings.matters: Unadjusted misstatements mean the financial position reported is misstated; £363k pension understatement and £136k debtor errors are individually material to budget decisions.
findings.figures: £136k NNDR provision error, £363k pension understatement, £589k projected creditor error; cumulative £643k
findings.quote: We identified a calculation error in the NNDR debtors provision... The pension fund auditor identified an understatement of the total fund assets provided to the actuary amounting to £17,551k. Based on the council's share of 2.069% this results in a £363k understatement.

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Senior finance officers posting journals without restrictions and users able to self-authorise their own transactions
findings.detail: The auditors identified that both the S151 Officer and Deputy S151 Officer post journals throughout the year without restriction, and that system users can self-authorise their own journals. From testing 113 S151-level journals, no impropriety was found, but the auditors recommend removing both these control weaknesses. This issue was also raised in the prior audit.
findings.matters: These control weaknesses create fraud risk and bypass segregation of duties; senior officers posting and self-approving transactions removes critical oversight over financial records.
findings.figures: 113 journals tested from S151-level staff (42 from Director, 43 from Deputy Director)
findings.quote: We identified that the S151 and deputy s151 can post and do post journals in the year. From our testing we have not identified any issues in these journals but we would not expect senior officers to have this level of access. We also identified that users can self-authorise their own journals.

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Bank reconciliations unreconciled for four months due to staffing shortages and new system implementation
findings.detail: The council was unable to fully reconcile bank reconciliations from October to February 2025. Auditors attribute this to personnel shortages and the introduction of a new IMS system. The auditor notes that although officers invested significant time, they remain unable to complete this basic control function.
findings.matters: Bank reconciliation is a fundamental financial control; inability to reconcile cash for four months indicates potential gaps in control over council cash and the ability to detect misstatements.
findings.figures: October 2024 to February 2025 (4 months)
findings.quote: While officers have invested significant time into the bank reconciliation work, the council was not able to fully reconcile the bank reconciliations from October to February; this is primarily due to personnel shortages and the introduction of the new IMS system.

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Value for money assessment fails; three significant weaknesses in council arrangements retained from prior year with member behaviour issues unresolved
findings.detail: The auditors are not satisfied the council has proper arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness. They have retained one statutory recommendation and three significant weaknesses from 2023/24. The statutory recommendation concerns member behaviour, specifically bullying and aggressive behaviour among some members that has persisted despite supposed implementation of prior recommendations.
findings.matters: A failed VFM assessment indicates the council may not have the governance or operational controls to manage resources properly; persistent member conduct issues raise questions about oversight and decision-making quality.
findings.figures: One retained statutory recommendation; three retained significant weaknesses
findings.quote: We are therefore not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. Our findings are set out in the value for money arrangements section of this report pages 70 – 72.

findings.paper_title: Teignbridge District Council - Audit Findings Report - 30-01-26
findings.headline: Fourth consecutive year of disclaimed audit opinion signals persistent control and assurance failures
findings.detail: The council's accounts for year ended 31 March 2025 will receive a disclaimed audit opinion, meaning the auditors cannot express an opinion at all. This is the fourth consecutive year this has happened. The auditors cite inability to obtain sufficient audit evidence on opening balances across multiple areas as the reason they cannot form an opinion by the 27 February 2026 backstop date. Previous years' qualifications on PPE and SANGS balances are cascading forward.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means financial statements are essentially unaudited and creditors cannot rely on external audit assurance; lenders need clean audit opinions as a basic governance baseline.
findings.figures: Fourth consecutive year; backstop date 27 February 2026
findings.quote: Owing to the challenges of undertaking an audit where the previous years audits were subject to backstop-related disclaimed audit opinions, we have been unable to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion in advance of the backstop date of 27 February 2026.

findings.headline: External auditor issued 6 Statutory Recommendations on member conduct and governance, indicating significant governance deficiencies
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's audit of 2023-24 accounts resulted in 6 Statutory Recommendations approved by Audit Committee and full Council in February 2025. These address member conduct issues, Code of Conduct procedures, constitution amendments, and standards compliance support. Statutory Recommendations represent the highest level of audit concern.
findings.matters: Governance failures increase risk of poor decision-making and financial misstatement, affecting lender confidence in the council's control environment
findings.figures: 6 statutory recommendations
findings.quote: The external audit resulted in 6 statutory recommendations approved by the Audit Committee on 13 February 2025 and full Council 25 February 2025.

findings.headline: External audit identified council's unsustainable practice of using Funding Reserve to plug annual budget shortfalls
findings.detail: Grant Thornton audit recommendation IR7 identified that the council had been depending on its Funding Reserve to close budget gaps. The audit recommended the council reduce this dependency and stabilize reserves over the medium term, indicating a structural budgeting problem rather than one-off pressures.
findings.matters: Using reserves to plug annual deficits is unsustainable; continued practice depletes reserves and leaves the council vulnerable to external shocks
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The Council should seek to reduce its dependency on the Funding Reserve to close budget gaps, then stabilise its reserves over the medium term.

findings.headline: Council has recognized a significant deficit in its Medium Term Financial Plan requiring Modern 25 savings programme, with final impact dependent on uncertain government settlement
findings.detail: The council acknowledges a significant unquantified deficit in its MTFP. It is relying on the Modern 25 modernisation programme to deliver savings, supplemented by business plan savings. The council awaits government funding settlement details to understand the remaining budget gap, as current figures are only modelled assumptions.
findings.matters: An unresolved structural deficit indicates uncertain financial sustainability and higher borrowing risk
findings.figures: Significant deficit (unquantified); Invest to Save reserve at £500k
findings.quote: We eagerly await the settlement from central government. We have modelled and assumed figures, but a big step towards understanding the future budget gap will be receiving actual numbers, hopefully before Christmas.

findings.headline: Annual net interest income forecast to decline by £502,000 to £1.49m due to Bank of England rate cuts
findings.detail: Teignbridge forecasts net interest receivable for 2025-26 of £1,493,212, down from £1,995,833 in 2024-25 — a decline of approximately 25%. The review explicitly attributes this decrease to lower interest rates following two Bank of England cuts from 4.50% in April to 4.00% in August. The average net interest rate earned in the first half was 4.25%, compared to 5.21% in the equivalent period of 2024-25.
findings.matters: For a finance director, this is a material loss of budgeted income requiring compensating savings or use of reserves. For a lender, it demonstrates the council's exposure to interest rate risk on its liquid reserves, though the council maintains substantial investments (£37.9m average daily lending) and sound treasury management.
findings.figures: £1,493,212 forecast (down from £1,995,833 prior year); base rates 4.50% to 4.00%; average earned rate 4.25% (down from 5.21%)
findings.quote: The interest forecast predicts total net interest receivable for the year of £1,493,212. This compares to £1,995,833 received in 2024-25. This forecast decrease is mainly due to lower interest rates.

findings.headline: Housing and homelessness service performance deteriorated, with six red RAG-rated indicators (up from five in prior year).
findings.detail: As of Q3 2024/25, the council rated six housing and homelessness indicators as red (representing worst performance), an increase from five in 2023/24. The auditor notes this has been partly driven by landlords leaving residential rental market for holiday accommodation, but also by issues with project completion timing. National legislation to speed up planning is being proposed, but current performance suggests service pressure.
findings.matters: Deteriorating housing performance in a council suggests pressures on a statutory service area and potential for this to drive future budget pressures or service failures.
findings.figures: 6 red RAG indicators for housing/homelessness Q3 2024/25 (up from 5 at end of 2023/24).
findings.quote: As at Quarter 3 of 2024/25, the Council RAG rated its performance as "red" for six housing and homelessness indicators. This is a deterioration on the position at the end of 2023/24, when five key performance indicators were RAG rated "red"

findings.headline: At least one high-profile building development capital project has a vacant Principal Officer role that has not been replaced.
findings.detail: The auditor identified that at least one significant capital project with a commercial partner has a vacant Principal Officer role because a retiree has not yet been replaced. The auditor also notes vacancies in support roles for the finance system project. The auditor raised an improvement recommendation (IR3) that resources for the Corporate Projects Board and Principal Officer roles on high-profile capital projects should be reviewed and increased.
findings.matters: Vacant key roles on capital projects increase delivery risk, delay, and potential for cost overruns; suggest capacity constraints affecting major project delivery.
findings.figures: At least one Principal Officer role vacant on high-profile building development. Vacancies in finance system project support roles.
findings.quote: we are aware of at least one building development project being completed with a commercial partner where the Council's role of Principal Officer is vacant because a retiree has not yet been replaced

findings.headline: Budget monitoring reports to members are infrequent, with no in-year monitoring reported between November 2024 and September 2025 outturn.
findings.detail: Budget monitoring data was reported to the Executive Committee only in September and November 2024, with no further in-year monitoring data reported. Year-end outturn was not reported until September 2025, leaving a ten-month gap without monitoring reports. The auditor notes that the administration chose not to have meetings in August 2025. CIPFA guidance states that quarterly reports to members on budget outturn and forecast are common, with some councils reporting monthly.
findings.matters: Infrequent budget monitoring impairs members' ability to take corrective action in-year and suggests weaker financial oversight and reporting discipline.
findings.figures: Budget monitoring reported Sep-Nov 2024 only; no reports Dec 2024-Aug 2025; outturn reported Sep 2025.
findings.quote: Budget monitoring data was reported to the Executive Committee in September and November 2024... However, no further in-year monitoring data was reported

findings.headline: Major finance system project delayed until late 2026 and now paused, impairing financial management capability.
findings.detail: A significant shared service finance system project (being delivered with Strata Service Solutions Ltd and involving Exeter City Council and East Devon District Council) was originally scheduled to go-live before 2024/25 but has been delayed until late 2026 and is now paused. The council had staffing vacancies in support roles for the project, affecting delivery. This system is critical for financial management and sustainability.
findings.matters: A paused major finance system upgrade suggests technical debt in financial management systems and indicates staffing or capacity constraints on major projects; impacts ability to implement stronger financial reporting and monitoring.
findings.figures: Finance system go-live originally before 2024/25; delayed to late 2026; now paused. Vacancies in Council support roles at various stages.
findings.quote: The go-live date should have occurred before the start of 2024/25 but was delayed until late 2026. Officers inform us that the project has now been paused

findings.headline: Transformation savings plan of £2.6 million is relatively modest and may be insufficient to close forecast budget gaps.
findings.detail: The council has a £2.6m 'Modern 25' transformation plan but the auditor explicitly describes this as 'relatively modest in value' and states that 'in the medium term, a higher value transformation programme may be needed to secure ongoing financial sustainability'. The auditor notes that delivering higher value savings requires the right skills and capacity, and LGA Peer Reviewers flagged concerns around skills, capacity and upskilling of staff. Only £89,685 was targeted for delivery in 2024/25 (though £207,815 was forecast to be delivered).
findings.matters: A modest savings plan against multi-year gaps of £11.7m means the council must rely on reserve drawdown and/or additional unplanned savings, increasing budget risk.
findings.figures: £2.6m Modern 25 transformation plan over two years. £89,685 targeted for 2024/25 (£207,815 forecast delivered). Forecast gaps total £11.7m over four years.
findings.quote: The present Council has a £2.6 million transformation plan that it is working through, but this is relatively modest in value... This is a relatively modest sum of planned savings. In the medium term, a higher value transformation programme may be needed

findings.headline: Member resistance to making savings in run-up to reorganisation, contrary to government guidance on stewardship.
findings.detail: At a Full Council meeting on 29 July 2025, some members questioned the need to make savings in the run-up to reorganisation, with proposed savings projects (such as public conveniences disposal) being challenged on grounds there is no point in helping the new unitary council. This stance contradicts MHCLG advice that councils must make decisions in the best interests of the whole area. In February 2025, sixteen members abstained from approving the 2025/26 budget due to concerns about debt levels, reserve dependency and affordability of capital projects.
findings.matters: Member resistance to necessary savings undermines financial stewardship and increases risk of budget pressures materialising faster than forecast.
findings.figures: 16 members abstained from approving 2025/26 budget. At 29 July 2025 Full Council meeting, members questioned value of savings in reorganisation run-up.
findings.quote: discussions indicated that some members feel making savings is no longer important in the run up to reorganisation. Proposed savings projects (eg for public conveniences) are being challenged on the grounds that there is no point in helping the new unitary council

findings.headline: Council faces multi-year budget gaps totalling £11.7 million forecast for next four years, requiring sustained reserve depletion to balance budgets.
findings.detail: The council forecasts budget gaps of £1.5m (2025/26), £3.8m (2026/27), £3.6m (2027/28) and £2.8m (2028/29). It holds £11.7m of earmarked reserves as at March 2025 to cover these gaps, but the auditor warns that if reserves are depleted beyond forecast, the council would quickly face using the General Fund Balance. The auditor's key recommendation is that the council should work to reduce dependency on reserves for balancing future budgets and seek to replenish reserves.
findings.matters: Sustained reserve dependency signals unsustainable budget balancing and poses lending risk if actual outcomes diverge from forecast or if additional pressures emerge.
findings.figures: £1.5m gap 2025/26 (7.5% of net service cost); £3.8m gap 2026/27 (21.8%); £3.6m gap 2027/28 (21.5%); £2.8m gap 2028/29 (15.1%). £11.7m earmarked reserves as at 31 March 2025.
findings.quote: The Council had £11.7 million of earmarked reserves available (as at 31 March 2025) to cover these gaps, but should that balance be depleted beyond what is forecast, then the Council would quickly be in a position of needing to use the General Fund Balance

findings.headline: Statutory governance recommendation retained on member conduct and decision-making.
findings.detail: The auditor retained a six-part statutory recommendation from 2023/24 addressing member behaviour, standards and decision-making, noting it has not yet been fully addressed. Between June 2024 and June 2025, 61 complaints were reported to the Standards Committee, with 30 from elected members. The auditor notes that lack of trust between members and officers may be underlying causes of poor behaviour and is undermining business as usual processes.
findings.matters: Member dysfunction and unresolved governance weakness directly affects quality of financial decisions, risk management, and the council's ability to pursue necessary savings and capital projects.
findings.figures: 61 complaints reported June 2024-June 2025; 30 from elected/co-opted members. One Group Leader reported difficulty disciplining their group.
findings.quote: our statutory recommendation from February 2025 has not yet had time to be fully addressed. It has therefore been retained... Lack of trust between members and officers may be one of the underlying causes of member behaviour contravening standards set out in the constitution

findings.headline: Rising capital costs and increasing borrowing costs are making it harder to achieve positive returns on capital projects.
findings.detail: The council notes that construction cost inflation (though smaller recently than previously) and the rising cost of borrowing combine to undermine the business case returns for capital schemes. The council models all capital projects with business cases and risk registers, but the deteriorating economics mean fewer schemes will meet required returns going forward.
findings.matters: If the council cannot achieve positive returns on its capital investment, it will either stop investing (affecting regeneration and services) or invest with negative returns (wasting resources and increasing future debt burden).
findings.figures: None quantified
findings.quote: Increasing costs for capital projects combined with increasing borrowing costs will challenge returns on capital projects and will require continual monitoring.

findings.headline: Treasury interest income is forecast to fall by £502,621 (25%) compared to 2024/25, due to declining base rates.
findings.detail: Base rates have fallen from 4.50% at the start of 2025/26 to 4.00%, with market commentators expecting further cuts to 3.75% by end March 2026. The council's forecast interest income is £1,493,212 against £1,995,833 in 2024/25. This is significant because the council holds substantial cash balances (£37-38m lent out or in call accounts each month) and is using these to avoid external borrowing, but the income from this strategy is declining sharply.
findings.matters: This reduces the council's financial flexibility and adds to the structural deficit problem. It also means the savings from avoiding external borrowing (currently £505,554 pa) will diminish as rates continue to fall.
findings.figures: Forecast interest income £1,493,212 vs £1,995,833 in 2024/25 (decrease of £502,621); base rate 4.50% → 4.00%; average lending rate to end September 4.25%
findings.quote: Forecast net interest receivable at £1,493,212 is forecast to be up £313,722 on the base income budget of £1,179,490...This forecast decrease is due to lower interest rates.

findings.headline: New Homes Bonus is being abolished with no replacement funding identified, and business rates retention is expected to be reset from 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council receives only one-year government settlements and has no clarity on funding beyond March 2026. New Homes Bonus — a material income stream — is anticipated to be scrapped. Business rates retention above baseline is expected to be reset next year, which will eliminate most of the gains the council has been making from this source. Funding reform is expected to take effect from 2026/27 but the council has not yet received detail of what it will look like.
findings.matters: The council is planning for a significant loss of revenue with no confirmed replacement, which is driving the medium-term deficits. Until government announces the detail, the budget for 2026/27 and beyond is incomplete.
findings.figures: New Homes Bonus scrapped; rates retention reset expected to eliminate pooling gains
findings.quote: New homes bonus is still anticipated to be scrapped with no alternative funding currently suggested. Estimated rates retention above the baseline and pooling gain is assumed to be reset next year as part of the current review and consultation into fair funding which will eliminate most of the gains made.

findings.headline: Council faces £3.8m deficit in 2026/27 and £3.6m in 2027/28, to be funded from earmarked reserves.
findings.detail: The February 2025 budget identified these deficits for the next two years. The council is currently running a £820k surplus in 2025/26, but this depends on a £1.5m planned drawdown from the Funding Reserve. The work being done through the Modern 25 programme and Ignite to find savings has not yet produced concrete figures to close the future-year gaps.
findings.matters: A multi-year structural deficit funded by reserves is unsustainable and indicates the council will need to either cut services materially or find savings that are not yet identified or committed.
findings.figures: £3.8 million deficit 2026/27, £3.6 million deficit 2027/28; £1.5m planned Funding Reserve use in current year
findings.quote: the February 2025 budget identified a budget deficit next year of £3.8 million for 2026/27 and £3.6 million for 2027/28 currently being funded by earmarked reserves

news_drafts.headline: £1m provision for Devon Local Government Reorganisation (April 2028) drawn from reserves intended for other needs
news_drafts.lead: A £1m future cost commitment reduces financial flexibility and, combined with the ongoing structural budget gap, constrains the council's ability to respond to emerging challenges over the next two years.
news_drafts.paper_title: Full Council - 202526 Revenue Capital and Treasury Outturn

news_drafts.headline: Structural budget gap of £1.1m forecast for 2026/27, to be funded from reserves and further savings identification
news_drafts.lead: Ongoing reliance on reserve drawdowns to balance budgets and the need to identify further efficiencies indicates a structural imbalance that may persist across the medium-term financial plan, affecting the council's financial sustainability.
news_drafts.paper_title: Full Council - 202526 Revenue Capital and Treasury Outturn

news_drafts.headline: Significant capital project slippage: £6.1m delayed across four major schemes
news_drafts.lead: Capital delivery slippage across named major schemes signals execution risk and suggests the council may struggle to deliver its expanded 2026/27 capital programme (£33.4m), which a lender would need to assess as funded and deliverable.
